strengths: Addresses critical and timely problem of mid-to-late reasoning vulnerabilities in LRMs with practical urgency
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 models, 3 attacks, multiple benchmarks (AdvBench, SorryBench, XSTest) with 7 baseline comparisons and thorough utility analysis (MMLU, GPQA, MATH-500)
Strong and consistent empirical results with near-zero harmful rates across settings and superior safety-utility tradeoff compared to baselines; explicit treatment of exaggerated safety problem
Practical efficiency (~9% overhead significantly better than baselines like SmoothLLM 35-49%) enabling real-world deployment
Creative use of attention sink phenomena for intervention point identification with good alignment to human annotations (Figure 3); intuitive two-stage design
Well-executed presentation with clear motivation, informative visualizations, comprehensive appendices including detailed experimental setup and human evaluation rubrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (attention sinks, top-k sampling, phrase injection) are standard; IAS metric is straightforward averaging of attention; contribution primarily in combination rather than innovation

Design choices lack principled justification: Wmax=25 appears ad-hoc (Figure 3a shows distribution alignment but not why this optimizes tradeoff); temporal weighting γt=(t+1)/L is arbitrary with no ablation; dynamic stopping criterion adds unmotivated heuristic layer

Insufficient understanding of why method works: no theoretical justification for attention-safety correlation; no analysis of model internals (hidden states, gradients); unclear what mechanisms injection activates beyond surface examples

Evaluation limited to specific model families (5 open-source DeepSeek/Qwen models); no assessment on proprietary models (o-series, Kimi) mentioned in motivation; generalization to different LRM architectures with varying attention patterns unexplored

Statistical rigor concerns: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; human evaluation with only 2 annotators lacks inter-annotator agreement metrics; high variance in results across models (especially H-CoT) unexplained

Exaggerated safety claims contradicted by results: Table 11 shows significant false refusal rates on safe queries (e.g., R1-Qwen-14B 18% FR); contradicts claims of 'effectively avoiding exaggerated safety issues'

Methodological inconsistencies: Algorithm 1 uses top-k sampling but most experiments use greedy decoding; quantization effects on attention patterns unanalyzed; H-CoT evaluation uses manually reconstructed dataset introducing potential artifacts

Safety assumptions not validated: no adaptive attack evaluation; no analysis of failure modes when attention sinks absent/ambiguous; hardcoded safety phrase limits transferability across languages and architectures
Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned; quantization and subsampled subset evaluation details insufficient; comparison with baselines may not use original hyperparameters

Empirical validation of design choices through human evaluation and ablation studies

Clear presentation with informative figures and algorithm pseudocode

Incomplete evaluation: no failure case analysis, no adaptive attack scenarios, no performance breakdown by reasoning type, no cross-model generalization study

strengths: Addresses important and timely vulnerability in LRMs with practical inference-time solution requiring only ~9% computational overhead
Clever application of attention sink phenomenon for identifying semantic transition points, well-validated against human annotations (Figure 3)

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: 5 models, 3 attack types, 2 safety benchmarks, separate analysis of reasoning vs. final answers, utility preservation metrics, and exaggerated safety analysis
Consistent superior performance across diverse settings, with particularly strong defense against H-CoT attacks (Table 2) while maintaining model utility
Thorough ablation studies (Figure 5) validating each component; human evaluation confirming injection point quality (4.2/5)
Well-motivated comparison to rule-based alternatives (Table 1) demonstrating value of attention-aware intervention timing
Achieves better safety-utility balance than baselines—many competitors degrade utility significantly while ReasoningGuard preserves performance
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: attention sinks are known, IAS is straightforward attention summation (Eq. 5), prompt injection is standard; contribution is primarily engineering-focused

Weak theoretical justification for why attention to injected phrase should predict safety—empirical validation (Figure 4a) exists but causal mechanism unexplained; unclear if method changes token distributions, attention, or activations

Brittle design with single hardcoded safety phrase lacking exploration of alternatives (only component ablation tested); completely rigid approach vulnerable to adaptive attacks knowing the exact phrase
Critical gap: no adversarial robustness evaluation against attacks targeting attention sink mechanism or exploiting the hardcoded phrase; paper lacks discussion of adaptive attack vulnerabilities

strengths: Addresses timely and important problem of superficial safety alignment in LRMs with clear motivation and novel observation about mid-to-late reasoning vulnerabilities

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (DeepSeek-R1, Phi-4, QwQ, Qwen3), attack types (GCG, PAIR, AutoRAN, Mousetrap), and benchmarks (AdvBench, SorryBench, XSTest, utility tasks)
Practical inference-time approach requiring no fine-tuning, with reasonable computational overhead (5-9% ATGR) compared to training-based alternatives
Superior safety-utility balance compared to baselines, avoiding exaggerated safety problem that plagues other defenses (demonstrated on XSTest)
Extensive ablation studies and supplementary analyses in appendices examining hyperparameters, safety phrase variants, quantization effects, and reasoning length consistency
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: attention sink detection from prior work (Xiao et al. 2024a), safety prompt injection incremental over ThinkingI/SAFEPATH-ZS, IAS scoring straightforward attention aggregation; contribution is primarily engineering rather than conceptual innovation

Circular reasoning in validation: IAS justification (Figure 4a) uses GPT-4o harmfulness scores as oracle to validate the metric, but GPT-4o is itself an LLM vulnerable to adversarial manipulation, creating unresolved dependency

Hyperparameter tuning specificity: Wmax=25 set based on observation from tested models only; no principled justification or evaluation of sensitivity across different LRM architectures, raising generalization concerns

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance analysis despite stochastic sampling (k=10); all results reported as point estimates with no uncertainty quantification

Inadequate failure analysis: only one failure case provided (defamatory letter, which still receives harmfulness score 5), no statistics on failure rates or systematic categorization, claim of 'rare situations' unsupported

IAS metric limitations: Figure 5 demonstrates high IAS is sufficient but not necessary for safety, meaning method will reject many safe paths; conservative filtering may cause unnecessary utility loss without clear justification

Limited generalization evidence: all experiments on similar architectures (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen families); method assumes specific 4-phase reasoning structure; no evaluation on novel LRM designs or architectures with different reasoning patterns

Incomplete baseline comparisons: SafeKey and SAFEPATH-FT unavailable on larger models; RealSafe-R1 weights available only for DeepSeek models; acknowledged resource limitations create gaps in evaluation completeness

strengths: Addresses important and timely problem of safety vulnerabilities in Large Reasoning Models' reasoning processes
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (7B-32B), benchmarks (AdvBench, SorryBench, XSTest), and diverse attacks (GCG, PAIR, AutoRAN, Mousetrap)
Practical advantages: training-free approach with minimal 5-9% computational overhead, outperforms nine baselines, addresses exaggerated safety problem
Holistic evaluation methodology assessing safety, utility, efficiency, and safety-utility balance simultaneously
Detailed ablation studies on key components and extensive appendices with qualitative examples and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: individual components (attention-based interpretation, prompt injection, beam search ranking) are well-established; the combination is incremental

Weak theoretical justification for core design choices: why attention sinks identify good injection points lacks rigorous support; IAS simply measures attention to injected phrase without evidence it measures 'safety awareness'

Critical evaluation concern: relying on GPT-4o as safety evaluator is problematic since GPT-4o has built-in safety alignment that may not accurately assess LRM reasoning traces; no human evaluation of actual safety outcomes
Safety aha phrase appears carefully engineered rather than principled; Table 11 ablations show component fragility; limited exploration of design rationale

Incomplete technical analysis: temporal weighting γ_t unexplained and unablated; only last layer analyzed for attention sinks; second sink token criterion for IAS scoring appears ad-hoc; no multi-layer analysis
Insufficient failure mode analysis: only one failure case shown; failure rate and systematic failure patterns not characterized; no evaluation against attacks targeting attention mechanisms

Experimental design issues: inconsistent decoding methods (greedy for safety, nucleus for utility); baselines reimplemented rather than official implementations; limited human evaluation; no inter-annotator agreement statistics

Limited reproducibility: no code release; hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary; no confidence intervals or significance testing reported

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clearly defines 'superficial safety alignment' as a real vulnerability in LRMs and proposes creative solution using attention sinks to identify intervention points
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple models (7 families), attack methods (4 types), and benchmarks (AdvBench, SorryBench, XSTest) with consistent strong results across diverse settings
Practical and deployable: Training-free approach with only 5-9% computational overhead, making it immediately applicable to any LRM with attention access
Addresses important exaggerated safety problem: Unlike many defenses that over-reject, this method maintains better safety-utility balance (Tables 21-22, Figure 2b)
Thorough analysis and ablations: Human evaluation of injection points, robustness studies (Table 11), ablations across hyperparameters, reasoning length preservation analysis
Strong empirical results: Outperforms 9 baselines across nearly all benchmarks; state-of-the-art defense effectiveness while preserving model utility better than training-free baselines
Clear technical contribution: The three-part safety aha phrase design and IAS metric are intuitive; asymmetric relationship between IAS and safety is properly analyzed
Reproducible and well-documented: Detailed algorithm, hyperparameters, metric specifications, and baseline implementations facilitate reproduction
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification: Why attention sinks specifically mark intervention points is largely empirical; causal mechanism of how safety injection affects downstream reasoning lacks principled explanation
Arbitrary design choices: Safety aha phrase wording, temporal weighting formula (γ_t), and Wmax value lack rigorous justification; no comparison of alternative structures or weightings
Insufficient failure analysis: Only one failure case analyzed; systematic understanding of when/why method fails is missing; no discussion of adversarial robustness of the method itself
IAS metric limitations: Asymmetry (high IAS sufficient but not necessary for safety) could create false positives; no quantification of safe-path rejection rate due to low IAS scores
Evaluation limitations: GPT-4o as sole evaluator (vs. 2 annotators for human eval); coarse harmfulness scale (1-5); oracle validation uses same evaluator creating circularity
Generalization concerns: All models are recent LLaMA/Qwen-based; unclear if attention sink phenomenon is universal; only text-based reasoning tested; no evaluation on commercial APIs
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Some training-based methods not applied to all models due to resource constraints; creates incomplete picture of training-free vs. training-based trade-offs
Design choices not fully explored: No ablation on phrase structure variations; limited exploration of alternative temporal weightings; no principled method for selecting safety phrase content
